pitfalls: Late bookings and presentation in labour wrongly inflate the denominator → apply the exclusion criteria exactly as the KPI defines them.
Results are authorised on time but not passed to the midwifery team promptly, so the clinical benefit is lost even when the KPI is met → add the communication step as its own template field.
Repeat testing after an equivocal result is counted as a fresh breach → track repeats separately from the initial screen.
Serology platform downtime causes a batch delay affecting many samples at once → note any platform outage dates when interpreting results.
Gains fade once the dedicated batch is deprioritised during staff shortages → make the exception report, not just the batch process, the sustained safety net.
pearls: Recruit the antenatal screening coordinator midwife and a biomedical scientist from serology/virology together.
This maps to the National Infectious Diseases in Pregnancy Screening Programme's own quality requirements, so the data has a second use beyond this audit.
Use the LIMS exception report as a live dashboard rather than a one-off manual pull.
Report separately for each of the four infections, since some (e.g. syphilis serology) may have different processing times than others.

pitfalls: Training certificates are held by individual staff members rather than centrally by the employer, failing the regulation's requirement → require submission of a copy to the central record as a condition of the training counting.
New starters and locums are not added to the training record promptly → build training-record creation into the pre-employment/induction checklist.
Records show that training happened but not what it covered, failing the 'nature of training' requirement → require a brief description or course title, not just a date.
Staff who have moved role (e.g. from operator to also acting as practitioner) are not flagged for additional training → cross-check role changes against training records annually.
Gains fade after a learning management system migration loses historical records → export and archive records before any system change.
pearls: Recruit the radiation protection supervisor and trust education/learning management system administrator together.
Use this audit to also identify any staff whose training has lapsed and needs urgent renewal.
Report the audit result to the trust's statutory and mandatory training compliance dashboard, since it likely already has a reporting mechanism.
Keep a simple named list of practitioners and operators, updated whenever the rota changes, to make future audits quick.

pitfalls: The 'separate discussion' happens in the procedure room immediately before sedation, which the standard specifically discourages → record the physical location, not just that a discussion happened.
Same-day add-on cases blur the distinction between initial information and confirmation → apply the emergency/unplanned exclusion strictly rather than stretching it to cover convenience add-ons.
A generic consent form is signed without evidence of a genuine second discussion → look for narrative evidence of the discussion, not just a signature.

Patients seen only briefly by a different radiologist than the one performing the procedure may not meet the standard's intent → record whether the confirming radiologist was the same person who performed the procedure.
Gains fade once the mandatory field becomes a box ticked without a real discussion → spot-check a sample against patient-reported experience where feasible.
pearls: Recruit the interventional radiology lead and a specialist nurse who runs pre-procedure clinics.
Use existing pre-assessment clinic letters as the source for the 'initial information' half of the audit.
Present findings alongside patient experience feedback on how well-prepared they felt for the procedure.
Keep this as a standing item in the interventional radiology multidisciplinary team meeting, not just a one-off project.

pitfalls: Staff disagree on which procedures count as 'complex' without a published list → agree and publish the list with radiology leadership before cycle 1.
A generic hospital consent form is used instead of a procedure-specific one, missing procedure-relevant risks → track use of the correct, procedure-specific form as a separate data point.
Verbal consent is documented in detail but no form is signed, technically failing the standard despite good practice → count only signed forms as meeting 'written consent' for this audit.
Emergency conversions from a planned to an urgent procedure blur the consent pathway → record these separately rather than excluding them silently.
Gains plateau below 100% once the list is published but not enforced → build the list into the booking system so a procedure on it cannot be booked without a linked consent form.
pearls: Recruit the interventional radiology lead and a specialist nurse or consent lead as co-authors.
Reuse procedure-specific consent form templates from surgical specialties as a starting point where suitable.
Present the audit alongside the library's own consent-documentation learning (procedure-specific forms work; teaching alone does not) to justify the chosen fix.
Track patient understanding of risks as a longer-term follow-on measure once form completeness is achieved.

pitfalls: The checklist is completed retrospectively rather than in real time, defeating its safety purpose → spot-check timing against the procedure start time where the electronic system logs it.
Staff view the checklist as a barrier for 'quick' procedures and skip it → apply it to all procedures on the interventional list regardless of expected duration.
A paper checklist is easily lost or left blank → prefer an electronic mandatory field that blocks progression to the next step.

The general anaesthetic section, largely irrelevant to most interventional cases, causes staff to disengage with the whole checklist → confirm the department is using the RCR-adapted version, not the unmodified surgical version.
Champions rotate without a clear handover, and the role lapses → build champion allocation into the weekly interventional list planning.
pearls: Recruit an interventional radiology consultant and the lead interventional radiology nurse/radiographer together.
Designate a champion for each list as recommended in published implementation experience with this checklist.
Use a clipboard or fixed location for the checklist so it is always available at the point of use.
Report near-miss catches attributed to the checklist (e.g. wrong side identified at Time Out) as a powerful qualitative measure alongside completion rates.

pitfalls: Staff assume a chaperone is 'obviously' not needed for certain examinations and skip documenting the offer → require the field to be completed for every examination on the intimate-examination list, with 'not applicable' as an explicit, reasoned option rather than a blank.
Patients decline a chaperone and this is not distinguished from 'not offered' → give both options explicitly in the template.
Locum or visiting staff are unaware which examinations are classified as intimate locally → publish and circulate the local list.
The field exists on paper but not in the electronic system used for most bookings → prioritise adding it to whichever system captures the majority of these examinations.
Gains are not sustained after a staff rotation → include the requirement in departmental induction for new radiographers, sonographers and radiologists.
pearls: Recruit a radiographer or sonographer who regularly performs these examinations as co-author.
Publish a simple, agreed list of which examinations count as 'intimate' locally to reduce ambiguity.
Present alongside patient experience feedback, since chaperone offer is a well-recognised patient dignity marker.
Keep the audit brief and focused, since this is a quick, high-value dignity-of-care check rather than a complex clinical audit.

pitfalls: A generic hospital leaflet is sent instead of a procedure-specific one, technically meeting a loose definition of 'written information' but not its intent → require the leaflet to name the specific procedure and its specific risks.
Late-booked planned procedures (booked less than 48 hours ahead) are wrongly included and unfairly counted as failures → apply the inclusion criterion strictly.
Patients report not receiving or not reading the leaflet despite a record that one was sent → consider a simple patient-reported cross-check for a subset of cases.
Leaflets are only available in English, disadvantaging patients needing another language or an accessible format → record whether an alternative format was needed and provided.
Gains fade once the automatic dispatch process is not checked after an IT system change → re-verify the automation after any booking system update.
pearls: Recruit a interventional radiology specialist nurse who manages pre-procedure information as co-author.
Start with the two or three highest-volume procedures to build the leaflet library quickly, then expand.
Ask patients directly (a brief survey) whether they felt they had enough information and time to decide, as a complementary patient experience measure.
Share the leaflet library with the pre-assessment or referring team so information can be given even earlier, at the point of referral.

pitfalls: Weekend and bank holiday surgery has no physiotherapy cover → negotiate 7-day therapy rotas with the therapy lead before cycle 1
Contraindications are recorded inconsistently or not at all → add a mandatory free-text reason field so 'not mobilised' always has an explanation
Small numbers if only complete NHFD-linked cases are used → include all operated hip fractures, not just those with full NHFD data
Definitions of 'mobilised' vary between a sit-out and a walk → agree and print one operational definition before data collection starts
Gains fade once weekend cover reverts → make the rota change permanent in the therapy job plan, not a temporary trial
pearls: Recruit a physiotherapy team lead and the orthogeriatrician as joint audit leads so the change survives staff rotation
Agree the operational definition of 'mobilised' (sit to stand, transfer, or walk) with therapy staff before collecting data
Use the existing NHFD extract to identify the sample quickly rather than searching EPR from scratch
Feed results back to individual consultants and therapy shifts, not just as a trust-wide average, to drive local ownership

pitfalls: Weekend staffing gaps are the commonest cause of missed days → confirm weekend rotas before starting
Patients who become medically unwell mid-stay may appropriately miss a day → record a reason rather than counting every miss as a failure
Documentation of 'seen but not mobilised' is easy to miss in free-text notes → use a structured daily tick box, not narrative notes, for data extraction
Staff may see this as a workload-driven target rather than a patient outcome → present length-of-stay and discharge-destination data alongside mobilisation rates
Long lengths of stay reduce the eligible sample → extend the collection window if fewer than 40 eligible patients are found in 3 months
pearls: Link this audit to the existing hip fracture pathway audit so both cycles use the same case list
Ask ward physiotherapists to flag missed days themselves during data collection rather than relying on retrospective note review
Present results by day of week to show where gaps cluster
Keep the daily task list active after the project team disbands by building it into the ward's standard operating procedure

pitfalls: Sputum volume/purulence is not always documented in a structured field → agree a simple nursing prompt ('sputum: none/scant/moderate/copious') before starting
Weekend admissions may wait 2-3 days for physiotherapy review → record the referral-to-teaching interval, not just whether teaching ever happened
Patients too breathless or drowsy to learn a technique are wrongly counted as failures → add an exclusion/deferred category with a reason
Teaching without device issue undermines the fix → audit both teaching and equipment provision separately
Staff may see this as duplicating existing physiotherapy referral practice → show baseline data first to demonstrate the gap
pearls: Involve the respiratory physiotherapy team lead in designing the sputum documentation prompt so it fits their existing workflow
Keep a small stock of PEP devices on the respiratory ward so teaching is not delayed by equipment ordering
Use the same COPD admission cohort as any existing pulmonary rehabilitation referral audit to save data collection time
Report results to the wider medical team, since sputum documentation is a doctor and nurse responsibility as much as a physiotherapy one

pitfalls: 'Falls risk' documentation is inconsistent across wards → agree a single falls risk flag (for example, a falls risk assessment score) before starting
Staff may equate encouraging activity with increased falls, causing reluctance → share evidence that inactivity, not appropriate mobilisation, drives post-discharge falls and deconditioning
Bed rest reasons are not always documented → make a reason mandatory whenever activity is withheld
Ward staffing pressure limits time for supervised walking → recruit ward-based therapy assistants for regular short mobilisation rounds
Improvement may not be sustained once the audit team stops checking → build the prompt into existing nursing handover checklists
pearls: Frame this as a deconditioning-prevention project, which tends to get more staff buy-in than a pure falls-prevention framing
Recruit a ward sister and a physiotherapist as joint champions before cycle 1
Use existing 'sit up, get dressed, keep moving' campaign materials rather than creating new posters from scratch
Track length of stay alongside activity rates, since the intervention is expected to reduce it

pitfalls: Each therapy discipline may record time in a different system, making totals hard to combine → agree one shared recording format before starting
Weekend and bank holiday staffing typically falls below weekday levels → report weekday and weekend rates separately
Patients who genuinely cannot tolerate 3 hours (fatigue, reduced consciousness) are miscounted as failures → record a clinical reason field
Recording therapy time without documenting content risks gaming the metric → also spot-check that time reflects active, needs-based rehabilitation, not passive contact
Improvement may fade if extra weekend staffing is temporary → secure a recurring weekend therapy rota, not a short-term trial
pearls: Use the stroke unit's existing SSNAP data collection processes to avoid duplicating data entry
Agree the shared timesheet format with all three therapy disciplines before cycle 1 so ownership is shared, not imposed
Present intensity data alongside length of stay and functional outcome scores to show the clinical case for investment
Nominate a stroke unit therapy lead to keep the timesheet running after the initial audit team moves on

pitfalls: Patients who move wards or hospitals before discharge are hard to track → use the critical care outreach follow-up list as the sampling frame
ADL impact is often assessed informally without documentation → provide a short structured template rather than relying on free text
Busy discharge processes can push the assessment out of the pre-discharge window → set a hard 72-hour trigger on the EPR
Onward referral (community rehabilitation, GP, outpatient follow-up) is easy to omit even when the assessment is done → audit referral completion as a separate field
Staff turnover on rotating ward teams may not know which patients had a critical care stay → flag ICU-linked patients on the ward handover board
pearls: Use the critical care follow-up service, where one exists, to help identify the sample and check onward referrals were received
Involve both physiotherapy and occupational therapy in designing the shared functional assessment template so it captures both disciplines' domains
Present findings jointly to critical care and general ward teams, since responsibility is shared between them
Keep the mandatory EPR trigger active permanently rather than as a time-limited pilot

pitfalls: Which patients count as 'at risk' is subjective without a documented short clinical assessment → use table 1 of CG83 as a structured checklist
The manual may be offered but not actually coordinated for 6 weeks → audit both the offer and the presence of a named coordinator
Patients discharged out of area lose follow-up continuity → record discharge destination and adapt the coordination plan accordingly
Staff may not know the manual exists if it has not previously been used locally → confirm a manual is available and staff are briefed before cycle 1
Low baseline awareness can make the first cycle very low, discouraging staff → present it as a baseline-setting exercise, not a failure
pearls: Base the manual on a published, validated self-directed rehabilitation programme rather than creating one from scratch
Identify a single named critical care outreach practitioner to coordinate all manual referrals so responsibility does not diffuse
Combine this with the pre-discharge functional assessment audit, since both draw on the same discharge population
Ask patients or carers at the 2-3 month functional reassessment whether they received and used the manual, to check the fix is actually working, not just documented

pitfalls: Non-physiotherapy staff completing the assessment may skip physical domains they feel less confident measuring → provide a simple, validated tool with brief training
Different services may use different tools, making results hard to compare over time → agree one tool trust-wide before cycle 1
Acutely unwell patients cannot safely be assessed for gait or balance → record a deferred/not-yet-safe category rather than a fail
Duplication of effort if physiotherapy and medical teams assess separately without sharing results → use one shared assessment form
Improvement gained during the audit period may lapse without an embedded prompt → build the fields into the permanent electronic template, not a paper checklist
pearls: Recruit a falls service physiotherapist as joint audit lead alongside the geriatrician or falls coordinator
Choose a quick, validated tool (for example, timed up-and-go) that non-specialist staff can be trained to use in one session
Present results split by setting (ward versus falls clinic) since completion rates often differ
Use the audit as an opportunity to formalise physiotherapy input into every comprehensive falls assessment pathway, not just document it

pitfalls: Home visits are cancelled if the patient is not in, wasting capacity → confirm appointments by phone the day before
Different therapists may use different or no validated tools → agree and print a single tool before cycle 1
Long waiting lists mean many referrals are still open at audit close → report both completion rate and median waiting time
Assistants delivering the assessment without documented supervision breaches the standard even if the visit happens → make supervision sign-off a mandatory field
Gains from extra capacity may be temporary if funded only for the audit period → seek a recurring establishment change if waiting times improve
pearls: Use the falls service's existing caseload system rather than building a new tracking spreadsheet
Agree with occupational therapy leadership which validated tool to standardise on before starting data collection
Recruit a therapy assistant champion, since much of the extra capacity this audit is likely to need will come from supervised assistants
Report waiting time trends monthly to keep momentum after the formal audit report is presented

pitfalls: This population is easy to miss because it falls between 'no action needed' and 'full comprehensive assessment' → make the eligibility criteria explicit on the GP template
GPs may not routinely document gait or balance impairment structurally → provide a simple one-line documentation prompt
Community occupational therapy capacity for lower-priority referrals may be limited → agree a realistic waiting time target with the service before cycle 1
Patients may decline a home visit they see as unnecessary after a single fall → record declines separately from missed offers
Findings may not generalise if only one GP practice is audited → sample from more than one practice within the primary care network
pearls: Work with the primary care network falls lead to identify the sample via a coded search rather than manual note review
Keep the referral pathway simple (a single click or form) to make it easy for GPs to use during a routine consultation
Track whether hazards found at these lower-risk assessments still lead to meaningful interventions, not just a completed form
Share results with the practice, since GPs are the ones who need to change referral behaviour

pitfalls: Coordinating diaries across three disciplines is logistically difficult → fix a single weekly slot in advance rather than arranging ad hoc
Joint sessions may happen informally without being documented as such → add a specific joint-session tick box to the shared MDT note
Staff shortages in any one discipline can cancel joint sessions first → monitor cancellation reasons separately from non-arrangement
Patients who are too fatigued for a longer joint session may be excluded inappropriately → allow a shorter, still-joint session to count
The fix may lapse once the weekly MDT champion moves on → build the joint-session slot into the standing MDT meeting template
pearls: Agree the joint-session slot with all three therapy leads before cycle 1, not just the audit team
Use the stroke unit's existing weekly MDT meeting to plan the following week's joint sessions rather than a separate coordination meeting
Track patient and carer feedback on joint sessions, since this is often the strongest driver of continued staff engagement
Keep the documentation simple (a tick box plus disciplines present) so it does not become a burden that gets skipped

pitfalls: Criteria may be genuinely assessed but not documented in one place → create a single decision form rather than relying on scattered entries
Time pressure to free beds can lead to the decision being made before all four criteria are checked → make the checklist a hard stop on the discharge order
Mental capacity to participate in rehabilitation can be confused with formal mental capacity for decision-making → define the term clearly in the checklist
Family discussion may happen by phone and go unrecorded → add a simple 'discussed with: date, method' field
Early supported discharge teams outside the acute trust may not see this audit as their responsibility → involve the community team from the outset
pearls: Design the four-item checklist jointly with occupational therapy, physiotherapy and the early supported discharge team so all parties recognise it
Pilot the checklist on a small number of patients before full rollout to iron out practical problems
Use the same case list as any hip fracture length-of-stay or readmission audit to show the checklist does not increase early readmission
Keep the checklist short (one page) so it is completed rather than bypassed under time pressure

pitfalls: ADL impact may be assumed rather than formally assessed → require a structured tool or checklist, not a general impression
Occupational therapy capacity may be limited on general wards → prioritise ICU-linked patients on the daily occupational therapy referral list
Identified needs may not lead to an actual referral → audit referral completion as a separate outcome, not just assessment completion
Patients discharged to a care home may have needs met differently → record discharge destination to interpret results correctly
A low baseline in the first cycle may discourage staff → present it as identifying an opportunity, not blaming individuals
pearls: Combine this audit with the wider CG83 functional assessment audit to avoid double data collection
Involve ward-based occupational therapists directly in designing the ADL section so it matches their normal assessment style
Track discharge destination and any early readmission alongside ADL assessment completion to show the clinical value of the fix
Keep a named occupational therapy lead responsible for the mandatory field after the initial project ends

pitfalls: Reorientation is often done verbally but never written down → provide a simple tick-box bundle rather than relying on narrative notes
Ward layout and side-room availability may limit what environmental changes are realistically possible → record what was feasible given bed availability
Occupational therapy may not routinely be involved in delirium care on general wards → create a clear referral trigger rather than assuming automatic involvement
Family involvement is harder to document when visiting hours or distance limit contact → record attempts to involve family, not only successful involvement
Care bundle completion can become a box-ticking exercise disconnected from actual care → spot-check a sample against direct observation or family feedback
pearls: Build on any existing delirium screening tool already used on the ward rather than introducing a separate process
Involve a ward-based occupational therapist in designing the environment checklist items so they are practical for the ward layout
Present results alongside length of stay and falls data, since delirium management affects both
Nominate delirium link nurses on each ward to keep the care bundle embedded after the audit team's involvement ends

pitfalls: Heel offloading equipment (boots, wedges) may not be readily available on every ward → confirm equipment stock levels before cycle 1
General repositioning may be documented without a heel-specific plan → make heel offloading a distinct field, not implied by general repositioning notes
Patients may decline or remove offloading devices for comfort → record attempts and reasons for non-use rather than counting these as documentation failures
Occupational therapy or tissue viability capacity to review complex cases may be limited → prioritise review for the highest-risk patients first
Improvement may not be sustained if equipment runs out → agree a recurring equipment budget line with the tissue viability service
pearls: Involve tissue viability and occupational therapy jointly in designing the offloading field, since both disciplines contribute to equipment decisions
Use ward equipment champions to check heel-offloading device availability alongside data collection
Present pressure ulcer incidence data alongside documentation rates to show the clinical case for the change
Keep a simple picture-based guide at the bedside showing correct heel offloading positioning to support consistent practice

pitfalls: Staff without podiatry training may feel unqualified to assess foot condition → provide a simple visual checklist (skin, nails, deformity, ulceration) rather than requiring specialist skills
Footwear may be assessed but not foot condition, or vice versa → record both as separate fields
Podiatry referral pathways may be unclear to non-podiatry staff → build a direct referral link into the assessment template
Referrals made may not be tracked to completion → add a follow-up field for whether the podiatry appointment happened
Low staff confidence in the first cycle may underestimate true completion → pair the audit with a short training session on the checklist
pearls: Ask the podiatry service to help design the simple foot-condition checklist so referrals are appropriately targeted
Combine this with the physiotherapy-led gait/balance/muscle strength audit, since both use the same comprehensive falls assessment template
Track how many referrals lead to a completed podiatry appointment, not just how many are made
Keep the referral link visible and easy to use so it survives staff turnover

pitfalls: Out-of-hours admissions may lack trained staff to perform the screen promptly → ensure all admitting nursing staff, not just stroke-unit staff, are trained in the screening tool
Medication is sometimes given orally before food or fluid screening is considered, and gets missed from data collection → explicitly define 'oral intake' to include medicines
A pass on a validated screening tool is not the same as a full speech and language therapy assessment → audit the screen, and separately track specialist assessment for those who fail
Staff may screen but delay recording the result, making timing hard to verify → use time-stamped electronic entries rather than paper charts where possible
Compliance may fall out of hours or at weekends → report weekday/weekend and in-hours/out-of-hours rates separately
pearls: Recruit the stroke unit matron and a speech and language therapist as joint audit leads
Use the trust's existing validated swallow screening tool rather than introducing a new one
Build the screening prompt into the same admission bundle used for other early stroke standards (glucose, positioning) to reduce duplication of effort
Report results at the same MDT meeting that reviews SSNAP performance so the audit becomes part of routine stroke unit governance

pitfalls: Onset time is often estimated or unwitnessed, complicating the 72-hour calculation → record onset time precision (exact, estimated, unknown) as a separate field
Speech and language therapy weekend cover may be limited → report weekday versus weekend screening rates separately
Communication screening may be recorded informally in ward round notes rather than the standardised protocol → audit for use of the named protocol specifically, not any communication comment
Patients with severe dysphasia may be hard to screen definitively → record 'screen attempted, inconclusive' as a distinct category rather than a straightforward pass or fail
The 72-hour deadline can be missed simply through delayed transfer to the stroke unit → track time from onset to stroke unit arrival as well as to screening
pearls: Use the same stroke admission cohort as the swallow screening audit to minimise duplicate data collection
Agree a single standardised communication screening protocol with speech and language therapy before starting
Display the 72-hour deadline visibly on the stroke unit's patient board so nursing staff can prompt therapy teams
Report results alongside SSNAP communication indicators so the audit reinforces existing national reporting

pitfalls: Patients transferred to a rehabilitation ward may lose continuity of speech and language therapy follow-up → include a handover trigger for modified-diet patients on transfer
Staff shortages can deprioritise reassessment in favour of new patient screening → protect reassessment capacity as a distinct caseload category
'Stable' is not clearly defined, so reassessment may stop prematurely → agree a working definition (for example, no diet change for 2 consecutive reviews) before cycle 1
Weekly reassessment may be recorded informally without a clear date → use a structured, dated reassessment note
Long lengths of stay create a large caseload that can overwhelm capacity → monitor caseload size alongside compliance to identify staffing gaps
pearls: Use the stroke unit's existing dietary chart as a simple prompt for when reassessment is due
Agree a shared definition of 'stable' with the speech and language therapy team before starting data collection
Present caseload numbers alongside compliance rates to support any staffing business case that follows the audit
Track diet upgrades as a positive outcome measure, showing the reassessment process is clinically meaningful, not just procedural

pitfalls: Referral may happen but the exercise programme itself may not start before treatment begins → audit programme start date against radiotherapy start date, not referral alone
Patients may decline the programme due to treatment burden → record declines separately from the service failing to offer it
Speech and language therapy capacity in oncology services may be limited → identify capacity gaps as part of the audit's pitfalls, not just documentation gaps
MDT outcome forms may not have a dedicated field, making the offer hard to trace retrospectively → create the field before, not after, data collection begins
Patients treated at a different centre for radiotherapy may fall outside local documentation → clarify pathway responsibility for shared-care patients
pearls: Work with the head and neck cancer nurse specialist to identify the patient cohort quickly from MDT records
Time the swallowing-exercise programme offer to coincide with the pre-treatment dental and nutrition assessments already built into the pathway
Present long-term dysphagia outcome data alongside offer rates to strengthen the case for embedding the change
Keep a simple patient information leaflet ready so the offer can be made and accepted at the same appointment

pitfalls: Voice change may not be actively asked about unless prompted → use a direct question in the follow-up template rather than relying on the patient to raise it
Patients may not recognise a gradual voice change as treatment-related → provide a simple patient-facing prompt or questionnaire before the appointment
Voice therapy referral pathways may differ between ENT and oncology-led follow-up → clarify a single referral route before cycle 1
Some voice change may be expected and temporary, leading staff to under-refer → offer therapy for persistent change beyond an agreed time point (for example, 3 months)
Low clinic time may limit thorough voice assessment → consider a brief validated voice-related quality-of-life screening tool
pearls: Use a short, validated voice-related quality-of-life question set to standardise assessment across clinicians
Involve the ENT and oncology follow-up clinic teams jointly, since patients may attend either
Track referral-to-first-appointment time for voice therapy as a secondary outcome
Keep the referral link in the clinic letter template so it survives staff rotation

pitfalls: A suspicion noted informally in ward round notes may not be recognised as needing referral → tie referral directly to the structured screening tool result, not free-text impressions
Weekend suspicion may wait until Monday for referral → report weekday/weekend referral timing separately
Referral may be made but the detailed assessment delayed by caseload pressure → audit both referral and completed assessment as separate steps
Mild or fluctuating symptoms may be under-recognised by non-specialist staff → provide brief training on recognising subtle communication difficulties
Duplicate referrals from multiple staff members may distort the true referral rate → count time-to-first-referral, not total referrals
pearls: Build the automatic referral into the same screening tool used for the 72-hour communication screening audit
Agree an escalation route for referrals not actioned within 24 hours with the speech and language therapy team lead
Report referral-to-assessment interval as well as referral rate to show the whole pathway working
Use ward-based posters or prompts to help non-specialist staff recognise subtle communication difficulties

pitfalls: Severity of aphasia or dysarthria may not be consistently graded, making the eligible population hard to define → agree a clear severity threshold or tool before cycle 1
Assessment may be deprioritised in favour of more immediate rehabilitation goals → build a caseload flag so it is not forgotten, not competing informally for attention
Aids assessed as suitable may not be provided promptly due to funding or equipment delays → audit provision as well as assessment
Patients discharged to community speech and language therapy may lose continuity → include a handover field confirming the assessment need is passed on
Family or carer engagement is often needed for technology use, and its absence can be mistaken for the patient's inability to benefit → record carer involvement separately
pearls: Agree a shared definition of 'severe' communication difficulty with the whole speech and language therapy team before starting
Use the caseload flag system already in place for other therapy follow-up tasks rather than creating a new one
Track aid uptake and use at follow-up, not just assessment completion, to show the change is meaningful
Involve community speech and language therapy early so continuity is maintained after hospital discharge

pitfalls: Mouth care is often delegated informally without checking staff training → build a simple training checklist into ward induction for stroke unit staff
Family involvement can be inconsistent if visiting hours are limited → record attempts to involve family separately from successful involvement
Mouth care charts may exist but not be completed consistently → use a structured chart requiring a signature at each episode
Patients who resist mouth care because of reduced consciousness or agitation are miscounted as failures → record refusals and adapted approaches as a distinct category
Aspiration pneumonia rates may have multiple causes, complicating outcome attribution → present mouth care compliance as a process measure alongside, not instead of, pneumonia rates
pearls: Ask speech and language therapy to provide a short, standard mouth care training session for ward staff as part of stroke unit induction
Use a simple laminated mouth care chart at the bedside rather than relying on the general nursing care plan
Track aspiration pneumonia rates over the audit period as a secondary outcome to strengthen the clinical case
Involve family members proactively by giving them a simple mouth care information leaflet on admission

pitfalls: Screening may be attempted but not fully completed (for example, weight recorded but height missing) → count only fully completed, scoreable screens as a pass

Patients unable to be weighed (bed-bound, confused) may be recorded as 'not screened' when an alternative method should be used → record use of alternative MUST methods (ulna length, mid-upper arm circumference) as a valid pass
Night admissions may be screened just after the 24-hour window due to shift patterns → report the distribution of screening times, not just a pass/fail cut-off
Screening completed but not scored or acted on undermines the purpose → pair this audit with monitoring of action taken on high-risk scores
Improvement may not be sustained without an EPR hard stop → avoid relying on a paper reminder alone
pearls: Use the trust's existing MUST screening field in the EPR rather than creating a new one
Recruit ward-based nutrition link nurses to champion the mandatory field change
Present results by ward and by day of week to identify where gaps cluster
Feed screening completion rates into the same dashboard used for other admission-bundle metrics so it becomes part of routine ward governance

pitfalls: High-scoring patients may be seen by the dietitian eventually but not on the same day → record the exact interval, not just whether action ever happened
Weekend screening may have no same-day dietetic cover → report weekday versus weekend rates separately and consider a nursing-led interim action for weekends
Some wards may have an informal local policy (for example, fortified diet menu) that is not documented as a formal action → make 'local policy action' an explicit, codeable option
Automatic referrals may generate an unmanageable volume for the dietetic service → monitor referral volume and dietetic capacity alongside compliance
Duplicate referrals for patients already known to dietetics may inflate apparent non-compliance → exclude patients already under active review
pearls: Agree the same-day interim nursing action (for example, starting food record charts and fortified diet) with dietetics before the automatic referral is built
Use the existing MUST screening EPR field as the trigger point rather than creating a parallel system
Track dietetic referral volume weekly during the pilot to catch capacity problems early
Report same-day action rates to ward sisters as well as dietetics, since nursing staff often make the first move

pitfalls: High-risk criteria may not be systematically checked before feeding starts → build a structured criteria checklist into the dietetic assessment
Estimated requirements may be calculated inconsistently between staff → use a standard calculation method agreed with dietetics
Out-of-hours feeding may start before dietetic review, at full rate by default → provide a simple out-of-hours prescribing guide for medical and nursing staff
Biochemical monitoring may be requested but results not reviewed promptly → audit both request and same-day review of results
Feed rate may be recorded on a nursing chart but not cross-checked against the prescription → use one shared, agreed feeding rate record
pearls: Provide a quick-reference refeeding risk card for out-of-hours medical staff, since risk is often first identified outside normal dietetic hours
Agree the standard requirement calculation and prescribing defaults with the nutrition support team and pharmacy together
Track biochemical abnormalities and complications as a secondary outcome to demonstrate the safety benefit of compliance
Keep a small dietetic on-call or telephone advice service, where feasible, to support out-of-hours refeeding decisions

pitfalls: Screening results may be documented in the EPR but not carried into the discharge letter, which is what primary care and care homes actually see → audit the discharge letter specifically, not the EPR record alone
Nutrition goals may be informal (for example, verbal advice) and not written down → require a structured goals field, not free text alone
Auto-population may fail if the discharge letter is generated before the final MUST score is entered → sequence the discharge workflow so nutrition data is finalised first
Community and care home recipients may not act on the information even when it is communicated → consider tracking whether GP or care home nutrition action follows, as a stretch outcome
High volume of standard discharge letters may make manual auditing slow → use a coded search for the mandatory field once implemented
pearls: Work with the IT/EPR team to auto-populate the discharge letter from the existing MUST record rather than requiring manual entry
Include this as a checklist item in the trust's standard discharge safety checklist
Present results alongside readmission data, since unclear nutrition handover is a recognised contributor to early readmission
Share results with community dietetics and care home liaison teams, who are the ultimate recipients of this information

pitfalls: Outpatient clinics often lack scales or a private space to weigh patients → confirm basic equipment is available before cycle 1
Nursing or clinic support staff capacity to add a new screening step may be limited → pilot in 1-2 high-yield clinics first, not trust-wide
Patients attending by telephone or video cannot be physically screened → exclude these from the denominator or use a self-reported alternative
A positive screen may not lead to a dietitian referral if no clear pathway exists in outpatients → agree the outpatient referral route before starting data collection
Clinics with high patient turnover may see screening as adding unacceptable time → use the shortest validated tool and involve clinic staff in timing it before rollout
pearls: Start with a clinic where malnutrition risk is clinically plausible and staff are receptive (for example, oncology or gastroenterology) to build a strong case study
Provide a simple self-completion weight-loss question card that patients can fill in the waiting room to save clinic time
Agree the outpatient dietitian referral pathway with the dietetic service before starting, so a positive screen has somewhere to go
Report time-per-patient added by screening, to reassure clinic managers ahead of wider rollout

pitfalls: High risk may be identified out of hours when specialist dietetic cover is unavailable → provide a documented on-call or telephone advice route
General ward staff may feel confident managing 'mild' malnutrition without recognising true refeeding risk → provide brief training on the box 1 high-risk criteria
Specialist involvement may be a single initial review without ongoing follow-up until stability → audit ongoing review, not just the first contact
Locum or rotating junior medical staff may be unfamiliar with the referral pathway → include it in induction materials
Nutrition support team capacity may be limited, especially out of hours → monitor referral volume and capacity as part of the fix, not just compliance
pearls: Provide a simple laminated card of the box 1 high-risk criteria for admission areas and out-of-hours teams
Agree an on-call dietetic advice arrangement (even a telephone rota) before rolling out the automatic referral trigger
Track biochemical complications as a secondary outcome to show the safety value of specialist involvement
Include the referral pathway in trust induction for new medical and nursing staff so knowledge does not depend on individual experience

pitfalls: Some trusts may not have a formally constituted nutrition support team, making 'review' hard to define → agree a minimum joint-input definition (dietitian, doctor, pharmacist) before starting where no formal team exists
Parenteral nutrition may be started out of hours before the team can review → audit the interval to first review, not same-day review alone
Referral may happen without a documented outcome → require a written review note, not just a referral entry
Complex feeding started on a surgical ward may not be flagged to the nutrition support team if ownership is unclear → clarify referral responsibility with surgical teams before cycle 1
Capacity of the nutrition support team may limit how many reviews can happen within 3 working days → monitor team capacity alongside compliance
pearls: Use parenteral nutrition prescribing records as the simplest way to identify the sample
Agree the automatic referral trigger with pharmacy, since parenteral nutrition prescriptions usually pass through pharmacy first
Present line-related and metabolic complication rates alongside review compliance to show the clinical value of the change
Keep the weekly nutrition support team ward round visible on the hospital's clinical governance calendar so it does not quietly lapse

pitfalls: Community dietetic and homecare services may vary in how referrals are received, causing delays → map the local referral routes before cycle 1
Discharge may be expedited under bed pressure before all community contacts are confirmed → make the checklist a hard stop on the discharge summary
GP notification may happen via a generic discharge letter without a specific enteral feeding flag → add an explicit enteral feeding section to the discharge letter template
Care home residents may have different notification pathways than those discharged to their own home → record discharge destination and adapt accordingly
Patients or carers may not retain the contact details given → provide a printed, single-page 'who to contact' card in addition to the discharge letter
pearls: Work with the homecare feeding company (where one is used) to build a standard discharge checklist together
Involve the community dietetic service in designing the checklist so referrals arrive in the format they need
Give patients and carers a simple laminated contact card, not just a paragraph buried in a longer discharge letter
Track unplanned readmissions related to feeding problems as a secondary outcome to show the value of coordinated discharge

pitfalls: Referrers outside the acute trust (GPs, community podiatrists) may not know the correct referral route → publicise a single, simple referral pathway across primary and community care
Weekend or bank holiday presentations may miss the 1-working-day target through no fault of the referrer → report working-day compliance rather than calendar-day compliance
Referral date may be recorded as the date the letter is typed rather than the date the problem was identified → clarify the start point as clinical identification, not paperwork
Triage delay may occur even when referral is prompt, if the foot service is under-resourced → audit referral and triage timeliness as separate steps
Different definitions of 'active' foot problem may be applied inconsistently → use the NG19 risk stratification definitions explicitly in the audit template
pearls: Agree a single, shared referral form and route with primary care, the emergency department and community podiatry before starting data collection
Recruit a podiatry team lead and a GP with an interest in diabetes as joint audit leads to bridge primary and secondary care
Track referral source to identify where delays cluster and target the fix accordingly
Report results to the local diabetes network, not just the acute trust, since most referrals originate outside hospital

pitfalls: Patients who do not attend routine diabetes reviews are systematically missed → track non-attendance rates and consider opportunistic assessment at any contact
Foot risk assessment may be recorded without formal risk stratification, making the record hard to audit → require the risk category as a discrete, codeable field
Care home residents or housebound patients may be excluded from clinic-based recall systems → arrange domiciliary foot assessment as an alternative pathway
Multiple providers (GP, diabetes clinic, podiatry) may each believe the other completed the assessment → agree a single named responsible service
A high proportion of 'not recorded' risk categories can mask assessments that were actually done but poorly documented → review free-text notes as well as coded fields where discrepancies arise
pearls: Use the practice's existing diabetes register and recall system rather than building a new one from scratch
Agree a single coded risk-category field with the clinical system supplier so the data is auditable going forward
Prioritise recall for patients not seen in the last 15 months to catch those falling furthest behind
Report results back to individual GP practices within the network to drive local ownership

pitfalls: Risk category may not be clearly stated on the referral, defaulting patients to a lower-priority slot → make risk category a mandatory referral field
Capacity constraints may mean the whole service is over target, not just poorly prioritised → report absolute waiting times alongside risk-stratified compliance to distinguish the two problems
Patients may cancel or rearrange their first appointment, extending the apparent wait → record patient-caused delays separately from service delays
Referrals from different sources (GP, hospital, self-referral) may use inconsistent risk terminology → provide a simple risk-category reference for all referrers
Improvement gained by re-prioritising existing capacity may simply shift delays to lower-risk patients → monitor low-risk waiting times too, to avoid an unintended consequence
pearls: Use the podiatry booking system's existing data fields to build the risk-stratified reporting rather than a manual log
Share risk-category definitions with all major referrers (GP practices, diabetes clinics, hospital wards) before making risk category mandatory
Present waiting time data by risk category monthly to the podiatry team so slippage is caught early, not only at re-audit
Use the audit to support any business case for additional podiatry capacity if absolute waiting times, not just prioritisation, are the underlying problem

pitfalls: Risk category can change between assessments, complicating which interval applies → use the risk category recorded at the earlier of the two assessments
Patients who miss or cancel appointments extend the interval through no fault of the service → record patient non-attendance separately from service delay
High-risk patients needing very frequent review (every 1-2 months) generate a large recall workload → ensure administrative capacity matches the recall volume before rollout
Recall systems may not distinguish moderate from high risk automatically → build risk category into the recall system as a discrete field, not a free-text note
Patients discharged and re-referred may show an artificially long interval → exclude re-referred patients or flag them separately
pearls: Build the recall system on the podiatry service's existing caseload database rather than a standalone spreadsheet
Agree recall administrative responsibility explicitly, since this task is easy to lose between clinical and administrative staff
Report interval compliance by risk category separately, since high-risk patients are most vulnerable to slippage
Use missed and rearranged appointment data to identify patients who may need a different reminder method (text message, phone call)

pitfalls: Heel offloading devices may not be readily stocked on general wards → confirm equipment availability with tissue viability before cycle 1
Foot risk category may not be documented for inpatients unless specifically prompted → link this audit to any existing inpatient foot risk assessment process
Discharge summaries may mention diabetes generally without a specific foot protection service notification → require an explicit, separate field
Patients transferred between wards may lose their heel offloading device without it being reordered → include a ward-transfer equipment check
Notification to the foot protection service may happen verbally or informally and go unrecorded → require a written notification, ideally electronic
pearls: Combine this with any existing inpatient diabetic foot risk assessment audit to use the same case list
Work with tissue viability to ensure heel offloading equipment is readily available on wards with high numbers of diabetes admissions
Build the foot protection service notification into the same discharge workflow as other community referrals, rather than a separate process
Track heel pressure ulcer incidence in this population as a secondary outcome to demonstrate impact

pitfalls: Ward nursing staff may perform minor debridement as part of routine dressing changes without recognising this as 'debridement' → define debridement clearly (sharp, mechanical, larval, enzymatic) in staff training
Out-of-hours or weekend gaps in multidisciplinary foot care service cover may lead to non-specialist staff stepping in → establish an on-call or escalation pathway for urgent debridement needs

Surgical debridement under a formal operative plan may be wrongly flagged as non-compliant → exclude debridement performed by the surgical team as part of an agreed multidisciplinary foot care service plan
Documentation may record 'wound cleaned' without specifying who did what, obscuring true practice → require role and technique to be recorded explicitly
Staff may be unaware of the restriction if it has not previously been enforced locally → communicate the standard clearly before starting data collection, to avoid appearing punitive
pearls: Provide brief training to ward nursing staff on recognising debridement and escalating to the multidisciplinary foot care service rather than proceeding themselves
Agree an urgent escalation or on-call route for debridement needs identified out of hours
Use wound photography, where available, alongside documentation to support quality review of debridement episodes
Present results supportively, focusing on system gaps (access to the specialist service) rather than individual blame

pitfalls: Acute Charcot arthropathy is rare, making a 2-week sample impossible → extend the collection window to 6-12 months to reach a meaningful sample

The condition is commonly misdiagnosed as cellulitis or a sprain at first presentation, delaying the referral clock → audit time from first presentation with red flag features, not only from confirmed diagnosis
Non-weight-bearing advice may be given verbally without being documented → provide a printed advice sheet that is given and filed as evidence
Emergency department staff may be unfamiliar with the condition → provide a simple red-flag recognition card for diabetic foot presentations
Small numbers mean a single delayed case has a large effect on the reported percentage → present individual case narratives alongside the overall rate
pearls: Use a multi-year or multi-site case series if the local trust sees very few cases in a short window
Provide emergency department and GP education on the classic 'hot, swollen, red foot with intact skin' presentation of acute Charcot arthropathy
Keep printed non-weight-bearing advice sheets and offloading devices readily available in the emergency department
Review every case as an individual learning event with the diabetic foot multidisciplinary team, given how rare and high-harm delayed diagnosis is

pitfalls: Patients may be discharged from acute Charcot follow-up once the episode resolves, without recognising ongoing high risk → make the high-risk marker permanent, distinct from acute-phase follow-up
Coding of 'Charcot arthropathy' may be inconsistent across systems, making the population hard to identify → cross-check podiatry, orthopaedic and diabetes clinic records
Patients who move house or transfer care may fall out of the local foot protection service without formal discharge being recorded → record transfer of care as a distinct category from discharge
Long time since the acute episode may mean deformity is under-recognised as Charcot-related by newer staff → ensure the permanent marker carries a clear diagnostic note
Small numbers make the percentage sensitive to a single lost-to-follow-up case → review each case individually rather than relying on the percentage alone
pearls: Use a permanent, clearly labelled flag in the podiatry electronic record rather than relying on staff memory of individual cases
Cross-reference orthopaedic, diabetes and podiatry records when building the initial case list, since Charcot patients may be seen by any of these services
Review flagged patients annually at a diabetic foot multidisciplinary team meeting to confirm ongoing appropriate review
Communicate the permanent high-risk status clearly in any discharge or transfer letter if the patient does move areas

pitfalls: Scans done elsewhere (private, another trust) are missed on PACS search: cross-check with the patient at clinic.
Small numbers if the surveillance list is short: pool 2-3 clinics.
Definition of 'on surveillance' can drift between cycles: fix the inclusion list before cycle 1.
Patients who died or transplanted in the interval should be excluded, not counted as failures.
A recall list only helps if someone actions the alert: name an owner.
pearls: Ask the hepatology secretary or specialist nurse to hold the surveillance list; they are often the best placed to run the recall.
Agree the definition of 'surveillance patient' (cirrhosis, not palliative, no transplant) with the consultant before starting.
Link AFP requesting to the same recall so both come as one task.
Re-audit before the surveillance list changes hands with rotation, and write the SOP into the department induction pack.

pitfalls: Patients diagnosed with cirrhosis incidentally (e.g. on imaging for another reason) can be missed from the hepatology new-patient list: cross-check radiology reports too.
Endoscopy waiting lists can push the true 6-month window out: record the referral date as well as the scan date.
Counting a beta-blocker started for another reason (e.g. hypertension) as meeting the standard is a common error: it must be started for this indication.
Losing patients to follow-up before the scan is done should be recorded, not silently excluded.
pearls: Agree with endoscopy in advance that new-cirrhosis referrals get a 'surveillance' priority code so they are not queued behind routine OGDs.
Have the MDT coordinator flag every new cirrhosis diagnosis in real time rather than searching retrospectively.
Present early results to the endoscopy unit, since they control the main bottleneck.
Keep the same 6-month reporting window across cycles so trends are comparable.

pitfalls: Numbers will be small in a single centre; consider a longer collection window or combining with a neighbouring unit.
Endoscopist availability for banding is a genuine, recordable constraint, not a data-collection failure: capture it as a reason, not a blank.
Distinguish surveillance procedures from emergency bleeds, which follow a different pathway and should not be pooled.
A drop in banding rates after a trained endoscopist leaves or retires needs a rota fix, not just re-teaching.
pearls: Agree the criteria for 'trained in banding' with the endoscopy lead before cycle 1.
Build the booking rule into the endoscopy referral form so it happens automatically rather than depending on memory.
Track which endoscopists most often defer banding, to target support rather than blanket teaching.
Keep the beta-blocker-instead option visible in the template, since NICE treats banding and beta-blockade as alternatives, not banding as mandatory.

pitfalls: This is a 2023 recommendation: some clinicians may not yet know it applies beyond variceal bleeding prevention, so expect a low baseline and plan teaching alongside the template.
Carvedilol needs caution in severe hepatic impairment (see the related safe-prescribing audit): don't count inappropriate starts as passes.
Distinguishing 'clinically significant' portal hypertension from cirrhosis in general needs a clear, agreed definition before data collection starts.
Heart rate/blood pressure intolerance stopping the drug should be recorded as a valid reason, not a failure.
pearls: Pair this audit with the safe-prescribing check (avoid carvedilol in severe hepatic impairment) so the same data collection covers both.
Brief the hepatology team on the 2023 change before cycle 1 so the low baseline reflects true practice, not confusion about the recommendation.
Use a pharmacist to help identify eligible patients from the clinic list in advance.
Track discontinuation rates at re-audit, since tolerability is the main barrier.

pitfalls: Bloods done close to, but not attached to, a clinic letter can be missed: search the laboratory system directly, not just letters.
Patients who miss appointments will have gaps that are not the team's fault: record DNA separately from a true miss.
A MELD score without an explicit action plan for a value of 12 or more is a silent gap: capture the 'so what' as well as the number.
Manual MELD calculation is error-prone: check a sample against an online calculator.
pearls: An auto-calculating field in the EPR template removes the main source of missed scores.
Ask biochemistry whether the LIMS can flag a MELD-relevant panel automatically for coded cirrhosis patients.
Use the audit to also check that a rising MELD triggers a specific action (more frequent review, transplant discussion), not just a recorded number.
Keep the definition of 'compensated' consistent between cycles to avoid population drift.

pitfalls: GP-issued prescriptions may lag behind a hospital switch: check the most recent dispensed item, not just the hospital letter.
Some patients are on carvedilol for a genuine cardiac reason agreed with cardiology: exclude these, don't count them as failures.
A single low blood pressure reading is not proof of harm: look for a pattern (hypotension, worsening renal function) alongside the drug choice.
This is a 2023 change: expect resistance from teams used to carvedilol as first-line for variceal prevention generally.
pearls: Run the alert past pharmacy before switching it on, since carvedilol/propranolol substitution needs a dose-equivalent plan, not a straight swap.
Use the hepatology specialist nurse to flag ascites severity accurately, since coding alone under-detects refractory ascites.
Combine data collection with the paracentesis/albumin audit, since it is the same patient list.
Re-check blood pressure and renal function trends at re-audit, not just the drug name, to show the change actually protects patients.

pitfalls: Severity classification (moderately severe vs severe) can be applied retrospectively and inconsistently: agree the Atlanta criteria definition with the audit team before starting.
Vomiting or ileus is a valid reason to delay feeding: record it as a reason, not a failure.
ITU and ward notes are often separate systems: check both for the true nutrition start time.
A dietitian referral made is not the same as feed actually starting: capture both timestamps.
pearls: Recruit the ITU dietitian to help identify eligible severe cases and confirm start times.
Agree the Atlanta severity definitions with the audit team in writing before collecting data.
Build the 72-hour target into the same proforma as antibiotic and fluid decisions, since these patients are seen together on ward rounds.
Re-audit after any nutrition team staffing change, since dietitian availability is the main driver of delay.

pitfalls: Distinguishing a genuine early infective complication from reflex prophylaxis needs the clinical picture, not just the drug chart: review the indication written at the time.
Antibiotics started for a co-existing infection (e.g. chest, urine) should not count against the standard: capture the stated reason.
A drop in appropriate use after a locum rotation suggests the order-set change needs repeating at induction.
Retrospective note review can under-detect verbal, unwritten justification: flag unclear cases rather than guessing.
pearls: Get antimicrobial pharmacy involved early; they usually already track inappropriate starts informally.
Make the order-set change the single fix, since the topic card shows teaching alone reached only 65% risk-stratification gains and no reported re-audit for antibiotics specifically.
Feed results back to the acute take induction so new doctors don't reintroduce reflex prescribing.
Track antibiotic duration as well as whether one was started, since stopping a wrongly-started course late is a second failure mode.

pitfalls: Numbers will be small in most DGHs; a longer collection window or combining a few years' cases may be needed.
Verbal advice given informally (consultant-to-consultant phone call) may not be documented: ask staff to write even brief advice calls in the notes.
Retrospective identification of 'complicated' cases relies on coding accuracy: cross-check with the radiology report for necrosis/collections.
Delayed recognition of the complication itself (not just delayed referral) is a separate problem worth flagging separately.
pearls: Agree the regional referral pathway and contact route with the specialist centre before starting, so 'discussed' has one clear definition.
Use the upper GI MDT as a backstop: any complicated case not yet discussed externally should be flagged there.
Keep a shared log of specialist centre discussions so this audit can be repeated quickly from existing records.
Feed learning back to acute surgical take doctors, who are often the first to see these patients out of hours.

pitfalls: Shared care with the GP means results may sit outside the hospital record: check the GP-shared record, not just hospital letters.
New-onset diabetes diagnosed opportunistically should be recorded and cross-checked against the recommended interval going forward.
A recent hospital admission with unrelated bloods can create a false sense that HbA1c is being monitored: check it is specifically HbA1c, not just glucose.
Patients who move between hospital and GP-only follow-up need the recall responsibility made explicit.
pearls: Write the monitoring interval explicitly into the GP discharge/shared-care letter (NICE also expects HbA1c and DEXA frequency communicated to GPs, rec 1.1.7).
Combine this audit's data collection with the bone density audit below, since both come from the same patient list and letters.
A single shared spreadsheet or database recall (hospital or practice-run) is more reliable than depending on individual clinicians remembering.
Re-audit after any change of pancreatico-biliary consultant or specialist nurse, since personal recall systems do not survive rotation.

pitfalls: DEXA scans done at another hospital or via a GP osteoporosis pathway can be missed on hospital PACS: ask the patient and check the national image exchange if available.
A DEXA report without a documented follow-up action for osteopenia/osteoporosis is an incomplete pass: capture both.
Waiting-list delays for DEXA are a system issue, not a data error: record the request date as well as the scan date.
Long gaps between clinic reviews can hide overdue scans: check the DEXA system directly rather than only clinic letters.
pearls: A direct hospital-requested DEXA recall avoids the extra step (and drop-off) of asking the GP to refer.
Pair this with the HbA1c audit, since both are follow-up-completeness measures on the same chronic pancreatitis list.
Agree with radiology a standing protocol for chronic pancreatitis DEXA requests so referrals are accepted without individual justification each time.
Feed abnormal results into a bone health pathway (calcium/vitamin D, bisphosphonate referral) so the scan itself changes management.

pitfalls: Patients who have already started a gluten-free diet before referral will have unreliable biopsies: flag and exclude or record separately.
GP referrals sent by letter rather than an electronic pathway are harder to trace: agree one referral route before starting.
A weakly positive result needing EMA confirmation (NICE 1.2.2) adds a step that can be mistaken for delay: record the confirmatory test date too.
Waiting-list pressure on endoscopy is a genuine constraint: separate 'referral made' (clinician-controlled) from 'biopsy done' (partly system-controlled) in the results.
pearls: An automatic referral trigger from the lab removes the main point of failure (a positive result filed without action).
Brief primary care on the 'keep eating gluten until biopsy' message, since this is a common patient safety-netting gap.
Track both referral and biopsy timeliness so any bottleneck (referral vs endoscopy capacity) is clearly identified.
Share results with the endoscopy unit, since a rise in referrals may need a dedicated slot allocation.

pitfalls: Many coeliac annual reviews happen in general practice, sometimes without a distinct template: check GP records, not just hospital letters.
Weight alone without a comparison to a previous value misses faltering weight gain or loss: record trend, not just a single figure.
'Considered' dietetic input can be interpreted loosely: agree what counts as documented consideration before starting (for example, an explicit yes/no with reason).
Patients discharged from hospital follow-up to GP-only care can fall out of any recall system: check both settings for the relevant year.
pearls: A single shared template usable in both primary and secondary care avoids duplicated or missed reviews.
Use the coeliac patient group/dietitian list, if one exists locally, to identify the full eligible population rather than relying on clinic attendance alone.
Bundle the pneumococcal vaccination check into the same template, since NICE links it to coeliac care specifically.
Re-audit after any change to the GP recall system or dietetic staffing, since these reviews often depend on one named clinician.

pitfalls: Serology requested by the GP rather than the diabetes team can be missed if only hospital systems are checked.
Symptomatic coeliac disease may have already prompted testing before the diabetes diagnosis: record timing relative to diagnosis, not just whether it was ever done.
A negative result does not exclude future risk: NICE also recommends re-testing if symptoms develop later (rec 1.3.4), which is worth a separate note in results.
New diagnoses made as an inpatient (e.g. with diabetic ketoacidosis) may have this step deprioritised: check both inpatient and outpatient pathways.
pearls: Adding the test to the admission/diagnosis order set is far more reliable than relying on individual clinicians to remember an easily-missed association.
Use the paediatric-to-adult transition list as an additional source of newly diagnosed young adults.
Share results with the diabetes specialist nurses, who often run the new-diagnosis pathway day to day.
Track outcome of positive results through to biopsy referral, not just whether the test was requested.

pitfalls: A TPMT sent on the same day as the first prescription, before the result is back, is a common near-miss: define 'before' as result available, not just sample sent.
Urgent starts (for example, at discharge) are the highest-risk point for skipping the check: flag these specifically.
Local laboratory turnaround time affects feasibility: know the turnaround before setting a hard-stop rule.
GP-initiated repeat prescriptions after a hospital start need the same rule applied, or risk restarting without a recent result after a long gap.
pearls: A pharmacy-enforced hard stop is more reliable than a reminder, since this is a genuine patient-safety risk, not just a documentation gap.
Agree an urgent same-day TPMT turnaround with the laboratory for planned starts, so timeliness does not become an excuse to skip the check.
Audit alongside the ongoing FBC monitoring measure below, since both come from the same thiopurine-start list.
Flag any deficient result found to the whole team immediately, not just recorded, given the severity of the risk it avoids.

pitfalls: Biologics given via homecare can be continued on a repeat-prescription basis with limited direct clinical contact: check the homecare database as well as hospital clinic letters.
A telephone or virtual review counts if it is documented with the required content; define this before starting so virtual clinics are not under- or over-counted.
Faecal calprotectin results sitting in a different IT system from the clinic letter can be missed: search the laboratory system directly.
Patients who are stable and rarely seen in person are at highest risk of an undocumented, assumed 'still working' continuation.
pearls: A prescribing-system alert tied to the homecare/biologics pharmacy record catches patients who might otherwise coast without face-to-face review.
Use IBD specialist nurses to run virtual reassessments by phone with a structured symptom and biomarker check, rather than requiring a clinic slot for every patient.
Track the decision made at reassessment (continue/stop/switch), not just whether one happened, to show it changes practice.
Re-audit after any biologics service reconfiguration, since responsibility for review can become unclear during service changes.

pitfalls: Weekend and night documentation is the most likely gap: check whether missed days cluster on weekends before proposing a fix.
Retrospective note review can undercount verbal ward-round assessments not written down: only count what is documented, and say so.
Small numbers are expected; consider a rolling collection over 12 months rather than a fixed short window.
A patient transferred to a tertiary centre mid-admission should have their local-stay days counted, not penalised for the transfer.
pearls: A single-page bedside chart used by both medical and nursing staff is easier to complete reliably than relying on free-text ward-round notes.
Involve the IBD clinical nurse specialist, who often already tracks these patients closely.
Pair this with the 72-hour escalation-decision audit below, since both use the same admission cohort and monitoring chart.
Feed missed weekend days back to the acute medical take handover process, not just the gastroenterology team, since cover changes at weekends.

pitfalls: The '72 hours' point can fall on a weekend when senior IBD input is less available: check whether delays cluster there.
A verbal decision to 'wait and see' without written reasoning is a common near-miss: require an explicit written plan even if the plan is to continue watching.
Small numbers are expected; combine data over 12 months rather than a short window.
Distinguish patients who improved (correctly not escalated) from those who did not improve but were still not escalated, since only the latter are failures.
pearls: A joint gastroenterology/colorectal ward round on or around day 3 for every acute severe UC admission is the single most effective fix reported for this kind of delay.
Build the 72-hour trigger from the steroid start time recorded in e-prescribing, so the prompt is automatic rather than manually tracked.
Share results with both specialties, since the decision genuinely needs both to be involved (NICE rec 1.2.21).
Track outcomes (colectomy rate, length of stay) at re-audit to show timely escalation is not just paperwork.

pitfalls: Surgical input may be genuinely not needed in every case: only count 'surgery not involved' as a failure if there is no documented reason it was safe to omit.
Out-of-hours admissions may only reach the on-call medical team initially: check whether delays cluster overnight or at weekends.
A surgical opinion recorded as a brief note rather than a full review still counts if it reflects genuine awareness and input: agree the definition in advance.

This audit works best combined with the daily-assessment and 72-hour-escalation audits, since they share the same patient cohort; avoid re-collecting the same admission list three separate times without coordinating.
pearls: A single combined data-collection sheet covering all three acute severe UC audits (this one, daily assessment, and 72-hour escalation) saves duplicate note review.
An automatic dual referral removes reliance on the medical team remembering to involve surgery early.
Use the IBD nurse specialist to flag every acute severe UC admission in real time so both teams are alerted immediately.
Present colectomy rate and length of stay alongside process measures, since joint working is intended to improve these outcomes.

pitfalls: MASLD is often diagnosed incidentally on imaging done for another reason (e.g. gallstones): a purely GP-list-based search will miss these cases, so also check radiology reports.
ELF may not be available in every laboratory: confirm local availability and, if using an alternative (e.g. FIB-4), record which test was actually used.
A steatosis report without a documented diagnosis of MASLD in the notes can under-count the true denominator: define inclusion criteria carefully with the audit team.
Following up on an abnormal ELF result (referral to hepatology) is a separate step from testing itself: capture both.
pearls: A reflex laboratory pathway (steatosis + diabetes coded → automatic ELF) avoids relying on individual GPs or hospital clinicians remembering the test.
Engage radiology to standardise wording that flags steatosis clearly in reports, since ambiguous wording is a common cause of missed follow-up.
Use this as an opportunity to build a simple MASLD register, which also supports the HCC/cirrhosis surveillance audits above if advanced fibrosis is confirmed.
Track the proportion referred on for advanced fibrosis, not just tested, to show the pathway works end to end.

pitfalls: A raised ELF result filed in primary care without hospital visibility is the main risk: a shared alert to both GP and a hepatology inbox closes this gap.
Local availability of ELF is limited to some laboratories: numbers may be small, so extend the collection period if needed.
A patient who declines referral should be recorded as such, not as a system failure.
