Distinguish a new ELF-based diagnosis of advanced fibrosis from a result in a patient already known to hepatology for another reason.
pearls: A direct laboratory-to-hepatology inbox alert for abnormal ELF results is more reliable than relying on primary care to always act on an unfamiliar test.
Agree a simple 'MASLD-advanced fibrosis' virtual clinic pathway with hepatology so referrals do not need a lengthy standard outpatient wait.
Combine with the ELF-testing audit above as two stages of the same pathway.
Publicise the ELF threshold and referral pathway to GPs, since MASLD referral criteria are still unfamiliar to many.

pitfalls: Retrospective identification of 'active infection' can be difficult without a systematic screen: define what counts as an adequate screen (cultures, ascitic tap, chest X-ray) before starting.
Numbers are likely to be small: extend the collection period to 12 months or pool across a network.
Steroids sometimes started urgently out of hours before a full screen returns: capture whether the screen was at least sent, even if results were pending.
A documented discussion of risks and benefits with the patient (also required by NICE) is a separate item worth tracking alongside the safety screen.
pearls: Build the checklist into the same order set as the discriminant function calculation, so the safety steps and the treatment decision happen together.
Involve microbiology/infection specialists in agreeing what counts as an adequate pre-steroid screen.
Track 3-month and 1-month mortality alongside process measures, since this is the clinical outcome the safety check protects.
Re-audit after any change in the on-call hepatology or gastroenterology rota, since urgent decisions often fall to whoever is on call.

pitfalls: Alcohol history documentation is often incomplete, making the denominator hard to define: agree a minimum threshold (for example, an AUDIT-C score or explicit units/week) with the audit team.
Repeat LFTs without referral is a common default: distinguish 'LFTs repeated' from 'referred' clearly in the data.
Other causes of abnormal LFTs (viral hepatitis, drugs, MASLD) need to be genuinely excluded, not assumed, before this pathway applies.
Patients who decline referral or engagement should be recorded as such, not as a service failure.
pearls: A shared primary care-hepatology pathway document, agreed in advance, avoids ambiguity about who refers and when.
Use the alcohol care team or liaison nurse, where one exists, to support engagement with referral for patients who may be ambivalent about it.
Track outcome of the specialist assessment (confirmed ArLD, alternative diagnosis, fibrosis staging) to show the referral changes management.
Re-audit after any change to community alcohol or liver pathway commissioning, since these referral routes can change.

pitfalls: Pain management is often escalated informally through primary care analgesia rather than referral: capture what was tried locally before assuming referral was appropriate.
Numbers in a single DGH will be small: extend the collection period or combine with neighbouring units.
Ongoing alcohol use complicates referral acceptance and outcome: record engagement with alcohol support as context, not as a reason to withhold referral.
A referral made but not yet seen (long waiting list) should be recorded as 'referred', with the wait time as a separate issue to escalate.
pearls: Agree the regional specialist pancreatic centre referral route and typical waiting time before starting, so expectations are realistic.
Loop in the chronic pain team locally as a bridge while a specialist centre referral is pending.
Track whether alcohol support was also offered alongside pain referral, since ongoing drinking undermines both problems.
Use this audit to also flag whether surgical options (see NICE NG104 on duct obstruction) were considered at the specialist assessment.

pitfalls: Patients too agitated to safely take oral medication are a genuine reason to start parenteral treatment first: record this as a valid reason, not a failure.
Out-of-hours decisions may default to whatever is easiest to draw up (often parenteral): check whether time of day predicts drug choice.

A general alcohol withdrawal order set without a specific delirium tremens pathway can blur the distinction between routine and DT management: confirm the diagnosis is explicit before including a case.
Reviewing the withdrawal regimen after DT develops (1.1.4.2) is a second, separate standard worth capturing alongside first-line drug choice.
pearls: A default order-set option removes the need for staff to recall the correct sequence under pressure.
Loop in liaison psychiatry or an alcohol care team, if one exists, since delirium tremens often triggers a specialist review anyway.
Use ward pharmacy to spot-check compliance in real time, not just retrospectively.
Track whether the withdrawal regimen is actively reviewed after DT develops, since this is often forgotten once acute treatment is given.

pitfalls: Early discharge is a common reason parenteral thiamine is stopped prematurely: a discharge plan should include continuing IM thiamine or an alternative if inpatient days fall short of 5.
'Suspected' Wernicke's is subjective: agree a working definition (any one of the triad, or high risk plus a clinical decision to treat) with the audit team.
Drug chart gaps (missed doses) should be distinguished from a deliberate early stop.
A switch straight to oral thiamine without any parenteral treatment at all is a different, more serious failure than stopping parenteral treatment slightly early: capture both separately.
pearls: Build a 5-day default course into the e-prescribing order, since manual daily re-prescribing is the main point where doses get missed or stopped early.
Arrange IM thiamine continuation in the community or via an alcohol liaison team for patients who could otherwise be discharged before day 5.
Use this audit's data collection to also spot-check that the correct high dose (BNF upper range) is used, not just that thiamine was given.
Share results with the emergency department and acute medical take, since under-treatment often starts at first presentation, not on the specialist ward.

pitfalls: A pre-endoscopy (admission) Rockall score is sometimes recorded instead of the full post-endoscopy score: check the field explicitly includes endoscopic findings.
Patients who have emergency surgery instead of endoscopy should be excluded, not counted as missing data.
Teaching-only interventions have repeatedly shown only partial, non-durable gains in this exact measure [2283]; plan for an electronic or template fix from the outset rather than teaching alone.
Endoscopists working across multiple sites may use different reporting systems: confirm the field is mandatory in all systems used locally.
pearls: An electronic action set embedded in the endoscopy reporting system has already been shown to work for this exact measure [5670]; replicate that approach rather than starting from teaching.
Auto-calculate the score from fields already entered (age, comorbidity, shock, diagnosis, stigmata) so completion does not add extra work.
Use the score to also verify safe early discharge of low-risk patients, not just as a box-ticking exercise.
Re-audit promptly after the template change, since electronic fixes in this specific measure have shown fast, large gains.

pitfalls: NSAIDs prescribed by a GP but not listed clearly on the hospital drug chart can be missed: check the admission medicines reconciliation carefully.
Distinguishing regular NSAID use from occasional over-the-counter use needs a clear history, which is not always well documented.
The discharge summary is the last safety-net point: a drug stopped on the ward but restarted by default on discharge (because it was on a repeat list) is still a failure.
Alternative analgesia not being offered can drive patients to restart NSAIDs themselves after discharge: consider tracking this too.
pearls: An e-prescribing alert linked to the GI bleed diagnosis code is more reliable than expecting every prescriber to remember on a busy take.
Make sure the discharge summary explicitly states the NSAID was stopped and why, so GPs do not restart it on a routine medication review.
Offer a paracetamol/weak-opioid alternative pathway alongside stopping the NSAID, to reduce the temptation to restart it for pain.
Distinguish and separately report low-dose aspirin (which NICE says to continue) so the two messages are not confused by staff.

pitfalls: Numbers are likely to be small in a single centre; extend the collection period to 12 months.
Rebleeding can be missed or delayed in recognition if nursing observations are not escalated promptly: consider auditing recognition time as well as treatment time.
Out-of-hours rebleeds may default to surgical referral without repeat endoscopy being considered first, which may be appropriate but should be a documented decision, not a default.
Distinguish a genuine rebleed from ongoing slow bleeding not yet controlled, which follows a different initial pathway.
pearls: Agree a clear definition of 'rebleed' (for example, further melaena/haematemesis with a haemodynamic change) with the audit team before starting.
A single-page escalation pathway readily available on the acute take and gastroenterology on-call phone line helps out-of-hours decision-making.
Track the interval from rebleed recognition to repeat procedure, not just whether one happened, since speed matters clinically.
Share results with interventional radiology, since they are part of the same escalation pathway for unstable rebleeds.

pitfalls: Terlipressin sometimes continues by default on a drug chart after endoscopy has confirmed haemostasis, simply because no one actively stops it: this is the main failure mode to look for.
A small number of patients need terlipressin continued for hepatorenal syndrome, a valid separate indication: exclude or flag these clearly.
Weekend handovers are a common point where a 'stop by day 5' plan is lost: check whether stop delays cluster around weekends.
Ischaemic side effects (digital, cardiac, mesenteric) are a rare but serious outcome worth recording if found, even though numbers will be small.
pearls: An e-prescribing hard stop at day 5 is a simple, durable fix that does not depend on staff remembering.
Make the endoscopy report a trigger: a 'terlipressin can stop now' flag when haemostasis is confirmed, linked to the drug chart.
Brief nursing and junior medical staff that terlipressin is not a default 3-5 day course regardless of endoscopy findings.
Track ischaemic adverse events over time as a secondary outcome measure, even if numbers are too small for statistics.

pitfalls: Acid-suppression started for a genuine indication (known peptic ulcer disease, reflux) should be excluded from the denominator, since ongoing treatment is then appropriate rather than a review failure.

Ward teams receiving the patient after critical care discharge may not know the drug was started as prophylaxis rather than for an established indication: make the reason for starting visible on the drug chart from the outset.
The drug can continue unreviewed all the way to hospital discharge and onto a GP repeat prescription: track this endpoint too, not just critical care discharge.
A documented review that concludes 'continue' without a stated reason is a partial pass at best: require an explicit reason.
pearls: A structured critical care discharge checklist is the natural place for this review, since it already covers other medicines reconciliation items.
Label the indication ('stress ulcer prophylaxis') clearly on the drug chart at the time of starting, so it is not mistaken for a standing indication later.
Loop in ward pharmacists to review stress ulcer prophylaxis specifically on step-down wards, as a safety net if the critical care checklist is missed.
Track whether the drug is still being taken at hospital discharge and, ideally, at a GP medication review, to close the loop fully.

pitfalls: Jaundice identified incidentally on blood tests (rather than clinically obvious) can be missed if only clinical documentation is searched: also check bilirubin results directly.

A clear, recently confirmed benign cause (known gallstone disease already under active management) should be excluded from the denominator, but this exclusion needs to be genuinely documented, not assumed.
ED presentations out of hours may default to 'admit and investigate' without an explicit 2-week-wait referral being made in parallel: check both routes.
Referral timeliness is only useful if the pathway itself is fast: also track time from referral to first MDT discussion, as the related audit found this step is also delayed [2287].
pearls: A hard-coded age-plus-symptom prompt in the referral system removes reliance on individual clinicians recalling the NICE criterion.
Agree with radiology/hepatobiliary surgery a fast-track imaging slot for suspected pancreatic cancer referrals, since imaging is usually the next rate-limiting step.
Present results to both primary care and the acute take, since jaundice can present in either setting.
Track the full pathway (presentation to referral to first MDT discussion to treatment) over time, since referral speed alone will not fix downstream delays shown in [2287].

pitfalls: An antibiotic continued because the patient develops a new, separate infection should be recorded as an appropriate continuation, not a stewardship failure.
Weekend cover can cause reviews to slip past 72 hours: check whether delays cluster there.
Distinguish antibiotics started specifically for GI bleed prophylaxis from those started for spontaneous bacterial peritonitis or another confirmed infection, which follow different courses.
Retrospective note review can miss brief verbal ward-round decisions: only count what is documented, and note this limitation.
pearls: A 72-hour hard-stop-style alert is consistent with the same principle already used successfully for surgical prophylaxis elsewhere; adapt that model.
Involve the antimicrobial pharmacist to review these patients proactively rather than relying on the medical team alone.
Pair data collection with the existing IV-antibiotics-before-endoscopy measure, since both use the same patient list.
Track total antibiotic duration as an outcome measure alongside whether a review happened.

pitfalls: Some patients are clearly unsuitable for TIPS (severe encephalopathy, advanced heart failure) and this should count as meeting the standard if documented, not as a missed opportunity.
Refractory ascites definitions vary; agree a clear, paracentesis-frequency-based definition with the audit team before starting.
Patients already listed for or having had a liver transplant assessment may reasonably have TIPS deprioritised: capture this context.
Retrospective identification from the paracentesis list may miss patients managed with fewer, larger-volume taps: cross-check with clinic letters too.
pearls: Use the paracentesis list itself as the simplest way to identify the eligible population, since these patients are already being tracked for another reason.
Build the TIPS/transplant discussion into an existing regular MDT rather than creating a new meeting.
Loop in interventional radiology early, since they will need to give a technical suitability opinion alongside the hepatology assessment.
Track outcomes (TIPS performed, transplant listed, or neither with reason) at re-audit to show the assessment step leads to a real decision.

pitfalls: A full, quantified drinking history (units/week and duration) is often missing from records, making the denominator hard to define: agree a minimum documentation standard before starting.
Some services already scan all heavy drinkers routinely and this may look like a ceiling effect: check local pathway assumptions before assuming a gap exists.
Elastography referred but not attended should be recorded separately from not offered, since these need different fixes (engagement support versus system prompts).
Patients already known to have cirrhosis do not need this specific test again: exclude them from the denominator.
pearls: Use the alcohol care team, where one exists, as the most reliable route to both take a full drinking history and refer for elastography in one contact.
A community-based (rather than hospital-only) scanning service increases uptake for patients reluctant to attend hospital appointments.
Track attendance as well as referral, since engagement is often the bigger barrier in this population.
Feed positive findings into the wider cirrhosis surveillance pathway audited elsewhere in this set.

pitfalls: Patients who stop attending follow-up (including due to ongoing alcohol use) are the group most likely to miss retesting, and also the group at highest risk: flag non-attendance rather than silently excluding these patients.
A retest done for another reason (e.g. incidental imaging) may satisfy the standard even if not labelled as a 'retest': check imaging history broadly, not just labelled follow-up scans.
Local availability of transient elastography devices limits capacity: record whether delay reflects service capacity rather than a process failure.
Patients who progress to cirrhosis between scheduled retests should be picked up by symptoms/blood tests, not solely by the fixed interval: note any such cases separately.
pearls: A chronic liver disease register with an automatic recall function is the most reliable fix; building this once benefits several of the audits in this set.
Community alcohol and liver clinics can help retain patients who might otherwise disengage from hospital follow-up.
Use this audit as an opportunity to build or refine a shared hepatology-primary care register, since retesting often depends on GP-hospital communication.
Report retesting adherence separately by diagnosis group (ArLD vs MASLD vs HCV), since engagement patterns often differ.

pitfalls: Confirming '3 months' abstinence' reliably (self-report versus biochemical markers) is itself inconsistent between clinicians: agree a documentation standard before starting.
Some patients are correctly not referred due to other contraindications (severe cardiac or psychiatric comorbidity): capture these as valid reasons, not failures.
Numbers will be small; extend the collection period or audit retrospectively over 24 months.
A patient who relapses during the 3-month period restarts the clock under most local pathways: record this clearly rather than treating it as an audit exclusion only.
pearls: A structured alcohol-abstinence tracking field (rather than free text) makes this measurable and repeatable.
Engage the regional transplant centre early to confirm the exact local interpretation of 'suitable candidate' criteria used alongside the NICE recommendation.
Loop in the alcohol liaison or addiction service, since abstinence support is central to whether patients ever reach the 3-month point at all.
Present outcomes of transplant centre assessments (accepted, declined, further tests needed) to close the loop beyond referral alone.

pitfalls: Shared-care monitoring split between GP and hospital can create gaps where each assumes the other is checking: agree and document one named responsible party per patient.
Missed appointments for blood tests are common and should be flagged for active follow-up, not just recorded as a gap.
A late-but-eventually-done blood test still represents a period of unmonitored risk: report both 'ever done' and 'done on time'.
Dose changes reset or alter the expected monitoring frequency; make sure the expected interval used in the audit matches current, not historical, dosing.
pearls: Use the exact structure that worked in a related paediatric audit: a shared-care guideline plus a tick-box monitoring proforma with all parameters listed together [2966].
A laboratory-generated automatic reminder is more durable than relying on either GP or hospital memory alone.
Make the responsible party for monitoring (GP vs hospital) explicit in every new thiopurine-start letter.
Track outcomes of any neutropenia detected, to show the monitoring system actually catches and acts on the risk it exists to prevent.

pitfalls: The discussion may happen verbally at diagnosis but not be written down: this audit measures documentation, and should say so plainly rather than assuming the conversation never happened.
GPs, not gastroenterology, usually administer the vaccine: the audit should track the discussion (specialist's responsibility) separately from vaccine administration (usually primary care's).

Patients already vaccinated for another indication (for example, age-related pneumococcal vaccination) should still have the coeliac-specific discussion recorded, since guidance and eligibility can differ.
A generic coeliac information leaflet mentioning vaccination in passing is not the same as a documented individual discussion: define the standard clearly before starting.
pearls: A single sentence and tick box in the standard diagnosis letter, copied to the GP, is a low-effort fix that also prompts GP action.
Pair the vaccination discussion with the annual review audit above so both draw on the same diagnosis-clinic dataset.
Consider adapting the invitation-letter approach already shown to work in the library [9569] as the mechanism for actually getting patients vaccinated once discussed.
Track vaccine uptake as well as discussion rates at re-audit to confirm discussion translates into action.

pitfalls: General ward MUST scoring may be completed routinely but not specifically prompt dietitian input for this high-risk group: check whether a score is acted on, not just recorded.
Nasogastric feeding can be difficult in patients with encephalopathy or agitation: a documented reason not to feed enterally should count as a valid clinical decision, not a failure.
Weekend admissions may have delayed dietitian input due to staffing: check whether delays cluster there.
Poor oral intake due to nausea or ongoing alcohol withdrawal symptoms needs separate management alongside nutrition, and should be recorded as context.
pearls: An automatic dietitian referral triggered by the diagnosis code removes reliance on the ward team remembering a nutrition-specific step amid other urgent decisions (steroids, infection screen).
Weekend and out-of-hours dietitian cover (or a clear escalation plan) is often the main practical barrier: check this with dietetics before proposing a fix.
Combine data collection with the pre-steroid infection screening audit above, since both draw from the same acute alcoholic hepatitis admission list.
Track nutritional status trends (weight, albumin) through the admission as an outcome measure at re-audit.

pitfalls: EPR build changes need informatics sign-off → agree the mandatory-field change with the CCIO before cycle 1 ends, not after
Junior doctors rotate before the fix embeds → nominate a pharmacist as the fixed point of contact
Free-text entries can be miscounted as complete → agree the definition of 'category used' with all data collectors before starting
Small numbers in a single specialty → collect from at least two wards to reach 40 cases
pearls: Recruit the admissions unit pharmacist as co-lead; they see the chart first
Agree the three-category wording with informatics before cycle 1 so re-audit uses the same EPR field
Present the before/after screenshots of the EPR field change at handover teaching
Keep the data collection tool to a single tick-box sheet so FY1s can complete it in under a minute per patient

pitfalls: Cases are hard to identify from coding alone → cross-check against adrenaline dispensing or resuscitation trolley records
Allergy clinic capacity may not match referral volume → agree an interim GP-led pathway with commissioners before cycle 1
Referral marked 'offered' without evidence in the letter → require the referral letter itself as the evidence source, not staff recall
Locum staff unaware of the pathway → include the referral step in ED induction
pearls: Identify a named allergy clinic contact before starting so the referral has somewhere real to go
Use the same anaphylaxis case list as any tryptase or auto-injector audit already running, to avoid re-searching notes
Show the ED consultant body the presenting numbers first, since they set the pathway
Keep the referral field as a single tick-box so it does not add time to a busy discharge

pitfalls: Trainer devices go missing or expire → assign restocking to a named nurse each month
Training documented as 'device explained' without naming the brand → define 'brand-specific' clearly for data collectors before cycle 1
Night shifts may lack trainer devices → check stock across all shifts, not just daytime
Patients too unwell at discharge to retain training → offer a follow-up call or allergy clinic re-demonstration
pearls: Get free trainer devices from the manufacturers' websites before cycle 1, at no cost
Recruit the ED discharge nurses as co-auditors; they already do the training
Link the audit to the two-auto-injector prescribing audit so the same case list serves both
Laminate a one-page technique card per brand for the discharge desk

pitfalls: Verbal advice given but not documented → require a tick-box, not free text, for this item
Leaflet given but not the anaphylaxis-specific one → check the leaflet code, not just 'leaflet given: yes'
Patients who leave against advice are missed → exclude self-discharges from the denominator with a documented reason
Paediatric and adult leaflets get mixed up in a shared ED → colour-code them
pearls: Print the leaflet directly from the discharge template so giving it is the path of least resistance
Ask the allergy clinic to review the leaflet wording before cycle 1
Combine this data collection round with the auto-injector training audit to save time
Keep a spare stock check as part of the daily ED safety huddle

pitfalls: Department pressure to discharge quickly → make the earliest-safe-discharge time visible on the tracking board so it is a system prompt, not a request
Symptom resolution time is often not documented precisely → agree a definition (last recorded abnormal observation) before cycle 1
Biphasic reaction history may be missed if old notes are unavailable → check the summary care record as well as ED notes
Small numbers if anaphylaxis presentations are infrequent → extend the sampling period to 6–9 months if needed
pearls: Recruit the ED sister in charge of patient flow, who controls the discharge decision
Use the same cases already being collected for the tryptase and referral audits
Present the observation-time calculation change alongside the current tracking board build, so it is one change, not two
Keep a laminated observation-time table at each ED bay as an interim measure while the system change is built

pitfalls: Auto-injector brand changes between reviews (supply issues) → check the brand on each review, not just that a review happened
Recall letters go unanswered → combine the review with an existing annual review (asthma, allergy) already attended
Practice nurse time is limited → use a short standardised checklist rather than a full consultation
Patients moving practice are lost to follow-up → check the repeat list is current before each recall round
pearls: Use free trainer devices from manufacturers so nurses do not need to buy them
Recruit the practice's allergy or asthma lead nurse to run the recall
Combine the review with the annual flu or asthma clinic to raise attendance
Keep the checklist to under 5 minutes per patient so it is realistic in a nurse clinic

pitfalls: FH may be diagnosed but not coded consistently → agree a single Read/SNOMED code with the practice before starting
Regional cascade testing services have long waits → record referral made, not seen, as the pass criterion
Patients decline referral → record as a documented decline, not a failure of the process
Small numbers in an individual practice → collect across a PCN if a single practice has too few cases
pearls: Agree the FH coding search with the practice's clinical informatics lead before cycle 1
Contact the regional genetics/lipid service to confirm their referral pathway and turnaround
Present the case for automation with real delayed-referral examples from cycle 1
Keep a running FH register so future new diagnoses are captured prospectively, not retrospectively

pitfalls: Family communication of risk is inconsistent → offer direct clinic-to-relative contact rather than relying on the index patient alone
Relatives live out of area → agree a shared-care pathway with neighbouring genetics services before cycle 1
Data protection concerns about contacting relatives directly → confirm consent processes with the clinic's information governance lead first
Long lead times for genetic results → record 'test sent' and 'result received' separately
pearls: Build the register prospectively from cycle 1 so future cohorts are easy to track
Involve the genetic counsellor early; they already manage family communication
Track by family, not just by relative, to spot families where uptake is systematically low
Share the six-month completion rate with the index patient's GP to prompt local encouragement

pitfalls: Reflex testing needs pathology IT and funding agreement → secure sign-off from the trust's cancer alliance before cycle 1
Biopsies with limited tissue may fail testing → record 'test attempted but inadequate sample' separately from 'not tested'
Abnormal results can be missed without a clear referral pathway → build the germline genetics referral into the MDT outcome form
Small numbers in a low-volume unit → extend to 9–12 months of cases if needed
pearls: Agree the reflex testing protocol with pathology, genetics and the colorectal MDT together before cycle 1
Use the existing MDT outcome form as the single source of truth for both testing and referral data
Present national uptake figures alongside local data to strengthen the case for reflex testing
Keep a running log of BRAF/MLH1 methylation results, since these determine whether germline testing is needed

pitfalls: Endometrial cancer is sometimes diagnosed on a small biopsy with limited tissue → record inadequate samples separately from untested cases
Genetics referral pathway differs between gynaecology and colorectal teams → agree a single shared pathway before cycle 1
Informing patients about hereditary implications needs trained staff → check rec 1.2 (informed consent and support) is followed alongside testing
Low case numbers in a smaller unit → extend the sampling period if fewer than 30 cases arise in 6 months
pearls: Align the endometrial and colorectal reflex testing changes into a single pathology laboratory business case
Involve the clinical geneticist in agreeing the referral trigger criteria before cycle 1
Use the gynae-oncology MDT coordinator as the single point of data collection
Share results with colorectal pathology, since the reflex testing infrastructure can be shared

pitfalls: Different calculators give different probabilities → agree a single approved tool with the genetics service before cycle 1
Older referral letters may not record a numerical probability at all → capture this as 'not recorded' rather than assuming non-compliance
Waiting list pressure may delay the offer beyond the clinic visit being audited → record 'offered' as the pass criterion, not 'tested'
Referrals from multiple specialties (breast, gynae-oncology, primary care) vary in quality → sample across all referral sources
pearls: Agree with the genetics service which calculator is their local standard before starting
Use the referral triage log as the single source for identifying cases
Present findings alongside the existing TNBC BRCA audit for a fuller genetics picture
Recruit a genetic counsellor as co-author for credibility with the service

pitfalls: Tumour (somatic) mutation results can be mistaken for germline and missed for referral → clarify in the laboratory report whether germline testing is also needed
Results reported to a non-genetics team who are unfamiliar with the referral pathway → include a referral prompt on the report itself
Patients who die or are lost to follow-up before referral → record as an exclusion with a documented reason
Multiple laboratories report to the same trust → check all reporting routes, not just the main cancer genetics lab
pearls: Work with the molecular pathology lab to build the alert directly into result authorisation
Agree with oncology and surgical teams who owns the referral action when a result comes back
Track time from result to referral, not result to genetics appointment, since waiting lists are outside the referring team's control
Share early results with the cancer genetics MDT to build momentum for the system change

pitfalls: Cardiac rehabilitation services may be commissioned mainly for post-MI/CABG patients, with heart failure referral pathways less established → confirm the local service accepts heart failure referrals before cycle 1
Frail or very elderly patients may be wrongly assumed unsuitable without a formal assessment → require a documented suitability assessment, not clinician judgement alone
Community or home-based options may not exist locally → record the format offered so gaps in provision are visible
Patients declining rehabilitation should be recorded as offered-declined, not as a system failure
pearls: Involve the heart failure specialist nurse, who already coordinates much of this discharge planning
Agree with the cardiac rehabilitation service in advance how they will handle a rise in heart failure referrals
Use the same discharge bundle build as the CABG rehabilitation referral audit already running, for efficiency
Report referral rate by referral format to identify where local provision needs to expand

pitfalls: Spinal cord injury presentations are infrequent in a single centre → extend the sampling period to 12–24 months if needed
Non-traumatic cases (for example from compressive pathology) may be referred later, from neurology or spinal surgery rather than the trauma team → include both referral routes
Staff unfamiliar with the NSCID system may default to informal telephone contact only → check both are properly recorded, not just one
Referral timing may be recorded on NSCID but not cross-checked locally → keep a parallel local log during the audit
pearls: Contact the linked Spinal Cord Injury Centre to confirm the agreed local referral protocol before cycle 1
Display the NSCID referral pathway and the direct SCIC telephone number in the emergency department trauma bay
Recruit the trauma coordinator or major trauma network rehabilitation lead as audit champion
Present findings to the regional trauma network, since this is a network-wide rather than single-hospital standard

pitfalls: Mobilisation date can be recorded inconsistently across therapy disciplines → agree a single definition (first out-of-bed sitting/standing) before cycle 1
Small numbers in a single specialist centre → extend the sampling period if fewer than 20 admissions reach mobilisation in a year
Weekly MDT diary pressure may push meetings later than planned → protect goal-planning meeting slots in the diary rather than fitting them around other business
Family/significant other participation may not be recorded even when the meeting itself happens on time → check both timing and participation
pearls: Use the SCIC's own MDT coordinator, who already runs the weekly meeting diary, as audit lead
Cross-check this audit against the referral-timing audit above to build a full picture of the SCI pathway from injury to rehabilitation
Present results alongside UKROC outcome data already collected by the centre
Keep a simple wall planner of mobilisation dates and due goal-planning meetings visible to the MDT

pitfalls: Family may live far from the specialist centre, making attendance difficult → accept telephone or video participation as equivalent to invitation and involvement
Patients may decline family involvement, which should be recorded as a valid patient choice rather than non-compliance
Small numbers of meetings in a specialist centre → extend the sampling period if needed
Invitation may happen informally by phone without being logged → require the invitation itself, not just attendance, to be documented
pearls: Combine data collection with the goal-planning meeting timing audit, since both use the same meeting records
Offer video-link attendance as standard for family members who cannot travel
Ask the SCIC's clinical psychologist or family liaison worker to help design the invitation record
Share this audit with the trust's patient experience team, since family involvement is closely linked to reported patient experience

pitfalls: Weekend admissions may have reduced therapy staffing → audit weekday versus weekend admissions separately
Patients with fluctuating consciousness may be hard to assess within the window → record a documented reason for delay where clinically necessary
TARN data entry lags behind clinical events → cross-check TARN records against ward notes for accuracy
Multiple specialties (orthopaedics, neurosurgery, general surgery) may each assume another team owns the referral → name a single responsible role in the trauma pathway
pearls: Use the existing trauma team activation checklist as the natural place to add the rehabilitation referral trigger
Recruit the trauma rehabilitation coordinator, who already tracks TARN data, as audit lead
Present the audit as part of the annual TARN peer review submission for extra visibility

pitfalls: Involvement may happen verbally at the bedside but go unrecorded → require a specific field, not reliance on general ward round notes
Family may be geographically distant or unavailable → accept telephone or video involvement as documented evidence
Junior staff completing the form may not know who was involved in earlier discussions → make involvement a discussion point at the rehabilitation MDT itself
Patients who decline family involvement should not be marked as non-compliant → record explicit patient choice as a valid reason

Ask the trauma rehabilitation coordinator to prompt involvement documentation at the weekly MDT

pitfalls: Incidents are under-reported when there is no injury log at all → introduce a simple paper or app-based log before cycle 1
Coaches and parents may pressure a return to play → back the pitch-side decision-maker with written club policy signed by all coaches
Volunteers may not recognise all concussion signs → provide a short recognition card as part of first-aid kit
Data collection depends on volunteers completing forms consistently → assign a single welfare officer to own the log

pitfalls: Access to a healthcare professional with concussion training can be limited in rural or amateur settings → agree a referral pathway to a local GP or sports medicine clinic in advance
Assessment happens but is not documented in a form the club can check → provide a simple one-page clearance certificate
Financial or time barriers to seeing a healthcare professional → make clubs aware of NHS and GP routes, not only private sports medicine
Players self-declare recovery without assessment → make the clearance form a condition of registration for that fixture
pearls: Partner with a local sport and exercise medicine clinic or GP practice willing to provide concussion clearance letters
Use the same incident log built for the removal-from-play audit to identify cases
Publicise the clearance requirement to parents and players, not only coaches, so it is understood league-wide
Keep the clearance form short so it does not become a barrier to a genuinely recovered player returning

pitfalls: Team sheets are not always retained systematically by amateur clubs → agree with the league to keep a central selection record
Competitive pressure (finals, promotion deciders) may tempt an early return → make the 21-day rule a league regulation, not just guidance, with a stated sanction
Cross-checking injury date against team sheets is time-consuming → digitise team sheet submission where possible
Players who play for multiple teams may return early via a different team → check league-wide registration, not just one club
pearls: Ask the league to formally adopt the 21-day rule as a playing regulation, giving the audit real teeth
Use existing fixture and team sheet records already kept for other purposes (discipline, results) to minimise new data collection
Share results with coaches at end-of-season meetings to reinforce the standard for the following season

pitfalls: Follow-up beyond the playing season can be lost if the player stops attending training → agree a follow-up method that does not depend on continued attendance (phone call, text)
Symptom self-report may be under-reported due to fear of missing further games → reassure players the check-in is about their health, not selection
Small numbers of persistent cases make percentages unstable → report raw numbers alongside the percentage
GPs unfamiliar with sport-specific return-to-play advice → provide GPs with a simple referral information sheet
pearls: Give welfare officers a simple three-question symptom check script to use at day 28
Build a relationship with a local sports medicine or GP clinic willing to see referred players promptly
Track persistent symptoms across a season to identify whether any single team or sport has a cluster
